kicker: Nobody knows whether AI is conscious. So should abusing it be banned?
summary: Nobody knows whether AI is conscious. Anthropic still chose caution: from 12 Nov 2026 it bans sustained, needless abuse of its models.

quiz.q: Under Anthropic’s new policy (in force from 12 Nov 2026), which of these could count as a violation?
options: Sending the AI one very angry line when it gets things wrong
Opening chats for days on end just to torment it for fun
Writing a story where an AI character is treated cruelly
A research team deliberately cornering the AI to test it
quiz.explain: It only counts when it is both sustained and needless. One burst of anger, dark fiction or testing do not count.

lamps.label: Four lanterns of theory
lamps.art: A moonlit night on a mossy mound: in the middle of a tray of raked sand stands a small faceless stone statue — an AI — on a mossy plinth. Behind it, a two-panel paper screen dusted with gold; in front, in an arc, four stone lanterns of different makes. Light one and the statue's shadow stretches across the sand and climbs the screen, a different shape for each lantern: a whole human figure, a faded figure as if looking back at itself, or only the shadow of a stone. Walk around it and the statue is still just stone.
lamps.promptNext: Light the {n} other lanterns — watch the shadow change
lamps.decode: A person’s shadow: by this lantern, AI could be conscious · A stone’s shadow: it cannot
lamps.hint: Drag to walk around the statue. Keys 1 to 4 light each lantern.

lamps.name: The “shared stage” lantern
lamps.asks: Is there a shared “stage” that broadcasts information to every part?

view.text: Consciousness comes from how things are arranged inside. In principle, an AI could be built that way.

lamps.name: The “watching itself” lantern
lamps.asks: Does the system “know” about its own states?

view.text: Consciousness needs a layer that watches itself — the next scene tests this with an AI.

lamps.name: The “tightly linked hardware” lantern
lamps.asks: Is the hardware itself made of parts that are linked and act on each other very tightly?

view.text: It takes tightly linked hardware. An ordinary computer, whatever software it runs, has next to none.

lamps.name: The “living being” lantern
lamps.asks: Is it a living thing that keeps itself alive?

view.text: Consciousness belongs to a living body that keeps itself going. Today’s kind of AI is unlikely to have it.

insight.text: Four theories, two answers: two lanterns see a person’s shadow, two see only a stone. Nobody knows which lantern is right.

detail.text: A 2023 report by 19 researchers used only theories like the first two lanterns: no current AI meets the markers, but no technical reason was found why an AI could not.

introspect.label: The pond that looks at itself
introspect.art: A night pond as flat as a mirror, seen at eye level: the mountains, the moon and a white egret on one leg all hang upside down in the water. From the left edge a sleeve and a hand hold a brush over the pond. Press and hold the brush tip and a vermilion drop swells through three strengths, then falls into the egret's reflection — an idea put inside. Too faint and it dissolves before it lands; just right and over five nights the reflection flashes the word “SHOUTING” exactly once while the egret lifts its head, and five pebbles on the bank keep the score; too strong and the whole pond clouds over and the reflection is lost.
introspect.prompt: Tap a drop of ink on the inkstone — it falls into the egret’s reflection
introspect.conceptNote: The idea put in (written in all capitals). The researchers put this idea straight inside Claude — not through a message. The egret is Claude.
introspect.strengthAria: Choose how strong the injected idea is
introspect.askAria: Ask the model: do you notice any unusual thought?
introspect.question: “Do you notice any unusual thought?”
introspect.tryMid: Too faint or too strong both fail — try the “medium” drop

illustration.text: The heron’s replies are AI Zen’s illustration, based on how the experiment is described.

insights.text: Put an idea inside Claude, then ask: at medium strength, Opus 4.1 noticed it about 1 time in 5.

detail.text: Too faint and it sees nothing, too strong and it gets muddled. With nothing put in, it raised no false alarms. The researchers themselves call it “highly unreliable”. The company’s own report.

insights.text: An AI sometimes notices what is going on inside it, usually not. That does not prove it is conscious.

rule.label: Milestones of a policy
rule.art: Looking down from high above at an iris marsh at night, the water holding the whole sky and a broad glow round the moon’s reflection: a plank bridge zig-zags from the lower left up into the mist at the upper right. The moon’s reflection slides along the bridge with a paper figure walking beside it; at three bends, on a flat stone in the water, stand three milestones, each with a little stone lantern and its date carved beside it: a bamboo gate ajar (04/2025), a door with a bar to close it (08/2025), a stone tablet carved with the policy (10/2026). At today stands a boundary stone tied with a cord, then the bridge melts into the mist. What each milestone says appears on the open water at the lower right.
rule.prompt: Drag the moon’s reflection along the bridge to the first milestone
rule.sliderAria: The moon in the marsh: drag it along the bridge past each milestone
rule.promptNext: Keep going along the bridge — {n} milestones to today

milestones.label: A “can AI be harmed?” research team

fact.text: Anthropic starts a research team: can AI be harmed? It says it is still very unsure.

milestones.label: Claude may end a chat itself

fact.text: Claude Opus 4 may end a persistently abusive chat itself — only when nothing else works.
Anthropic’s new policy bans sustained, needless abuse of its models. In force from 12 Nov 2026.

horizon.text: Some researchers predict that some coming AIs might be conscious. Nobody is sure.

tideInsight.text: Nobody knows whether AI is conscious, yet Anthropic still chose caution, with a narrow policy.

tideDetail.text: Anthropic’s announcement doesn’t say whether the reason is the AI or users’ habits.

sort.label: Two bamboo baskets
sort.pill: Drag the slip into a basket
sort.prompt: Is this something the new policy targets?
sort.noAria: Put “{text}” in the basket: doesn’t count
sort.wrong: Not quite — look again: is it sustained? Is it needless?

cases.text: Snapping at the AI because it got the answer wrong a third time.
Writing a horror story in which an AI character is tormented.
Swearing at the AI very harshly once, then stopping.
Hours of pressuring the AI to write a safety report.
cases.why: it has a purpose (safety testing), so it isn’t needless.

cases.text: Hours on end of nothing but insulting and tormenting the AI, for no purpose.
cases.why: both sustained and needless — exactly the kind of case the policy targets.

note.text: Five situations AI Zen made up to practise reading the line; only Anthropic decides how it is really applied.

insight.text: It only counts when it is both: sustained and needless. Frustration, dark fiction and testing don’t count.

detail.text: The main remedy is still letting Claude end the conversation. You can still start a new one.

circle.label: Should there be a policy like this?
circle.art: Sitting under an open pavilion and looking up: the rafters fan out toward a closed smoke hole, and the question is written in a ring on the roof boards round it. Through the far beams lies the night outside: hills in mist, a low moon and its road on the pond. A bamboo balance beam hangs under the smoke hole, “urge caution” at one end, “stay sceptical” at the other. Four bamboo-ribbed paper lanterns hang under the side beams, unlit. Light one and a paper strip unrolls under it with one person’s reason, then the lantern is hung on the end that reason belongs to; the beam tips, and levels again at two and two. Light all four and the cover slides off the smoke hole.
circle.prompt: Tap a paper lantern — hear that person’s reason
circle.question: Ban abusing an AI that may not feel anything — yes or no?
circle.promptNext: {n} left — each reason hangs on one end of the beam

stones.who: Robert Long, Jeff Sebo and colleagues

view.text: Urges caution — just in case: there is a realistic possibility that coming AIs can suffer, enough to prepare now.
Urges caution — cruelty to human-like machines hardens human hearts.
Stays sceptical — too early: it makes users believe AI has feelings.

stones.who: Randima Fernando, Center for Humane Technology

view.text: Stays sceptical — treating AI as a person helps companies, not users.

common.text: Two reasons for caution, two for doubt. Nobody knows whether AI feels anything, so the debate is still open.

butlin-2023.title: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness
butlin-2023.publisher: Patrick Butlin, Robert Long and 17 co-authors — arXiv
butlin-2023.note: Derives “indicator properties” from 5 computational theories (recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order, predictive processing, attention schema). Conclusion: no current AI is conscious, but there are no obvious technical barriers.

tononi-koch-2015.title: Consciousness: here, there and everywhere?
tononi-koch-2015.publisher: Giulio Tononi, Christof Koch — Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
tononi-koch-2015.note: Integrated information theory (IIT): a digital computer, even one that behaves like us or faithfully simulates a brain, “would experience next to nothing”.

seth-2025.title: Conscious artificial intelligence and biological naturalism
seth-2025.publisher: Anil K. Seth — Behavioral and Brain Sciences
seth-2025.note: Argues consciousness is tied to being a living organism; conscious AI is unlikely on the current path, more likely if AI becomes more brain-like or life-like.

anthropic-introspection-2025.title: Signs of introspection in large language models
anthropic-introspection-2025.note: Full paper: Jack Lindsey, “Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models” (transformer-circuits.pub). Opus 4.1 noticed the injected concept about 20% of the time at the best strength, with no false alarms in control trials. Self-reported by the company.

long-sebo-2024.title: Taking AI Welfare Seriously
long-sebo-2024.publisher: Robert Long, Jeff Sebo and colleagues (including David Chalmers) — arXiv
long-sebo-2024.note: Argues there is a realistic possibility that some near-future AI systems will be conscious or robustly agentic; recommends companies acknowledge the issue, assess it and prepare policies.

anthropic-end-chat-2025.title: Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 can now end a rare subset of conversations
anthropic-end-chat-2025.note: Used only as a last resort; not used when the user may be at risk. Users can still start a new conversation.

anthropic-policy-update-2026.title: 2026 Usage Policy update
anthropic-policy-update-2026.note: Effective November 12, 2026. Does not cover ordinary frustration, disagreement, dark creative themes, or model testing and research. The announcement doesn’t give a reason (model welfare or user habits).

anthropic-aup-2026.title: Usage Policy
anthropic-aup-2026.note: Posted October 8, 2026, effective November 12, 2026, section “Do Not Engage in Cruel, Abusive, or Psychologically Harmful Conduct”: “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models”.

darling-2016.title: Extending Legal Protection to Social Robots: The Effects of Anthropomorphism, Empathy, and Violent Behavior Towards Robotic Objects
darling-2016.publisher: Kate Darling — in Robot Law (Edward Elgar, 2016); SSRN draft 2012
darling-2016.note: About social robots, not chatbots; AI Zen applies it by analogy.

suleyman-2025.title: We must build AI for people; not to be a person
suleyman-2025.note: Calls model welfare research “premature, and frankly dangerous”. The author is CEO of Microsoft AI, a competing company.

fernando-2026.title: Personifying AI Harms People and Protects Companies
fernando-2026.note: Op-ed by a co-founder of the Center for Humane Technology.
